content:
Week 1 - JPA Basics # In the first week I worked with JPA and learned how Java can work together with a database.
The main thing I learned was ORM. Instead of writing SQL all the time, I can create Java classes that represent tables in the database. JPA and Hibernate then handle a lot of the connection between the Java code and the database.
I also learned how to create entities using annotations like @Entity, @Id and @GeneratedValue.
Another important part was CRUD, where I worked with creating, reading, updating and deleting data. I used EntityManager for this and also learned about the DAO pattern, so the database code can be kept separate from the rest of the application.
We also worked a bit with JPQL and Lombok. JPQL is used to query entities instead of working directly with database tables, and Lombok helps remove some repeated code like getters, setters and constructors.
Overall, this week helped me understand JPA better and how it can make it easier to work with databases in Java.
Exercises # During the week I worked on different exercises to practice JPA and database operations. One of the exercises was pushed on github as the “Codelab” exercise every wednesday.

content:
Week 2 - JPA Relations # In week 2 I continued working with JPA, but this time the main focus was relationships between entities.
I learned about the different types of JPA relationships such as @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne and @ManyToMany. These relations are used when different entities in the database need to be connected to each other.
One example I worked with was a student and course system, where multiple students can belong to one course. For this I used a @ManyToOne relation from the Student entity to the Course entity.
I also learned more about unidirectional and bidirectional relationships. This helped me understand that a relationship does not always need to work both ways, and that it is often better to keep the relations as simple as possible.
Another topic was cascade types, which control what should happen to related entities when an entity is created, updated or deleted. I learned that cascade should be used carefully and only when it makes sense.
We also continued working with DAO classes and JPQL to save, update and retrieve related data from the database.
Overall, this week gave me a better understanding of how entities can be connected and how relationships between database tables can be represented in Java whereas before we have only worked on this in databases.
Exercises # During the week I worked with JPA relations in a small student, course and teacher system.
Week 2 exercises on GitHub
title: Week 2 - JPA Relations

content:
Week 3 - Data Integration # In week 3 I worked with data integration and learned how to get data from an external API and use it in a Java application.
I worked with the TMDB API, where I used HttpClient to send requests and get movie data back as JSON.
I also learned how DTOs can be used to only keep the data I actually need from the API. In my exercise I used classes like MovieDTO and MovieResponseDTO for this.
Another thing I worked with was Jackson and ObjectMapper, which makes it possible to convert JSON into Java objects. This made the API data much easier to work with in the code.
I also learned that API keys should not be written directly in the code or pushed to GitHub, so they can instead be stored as environment variables.
In my exercise I created a MovieService that was responsible for fetching and working with movie data from the API.
Overall, this week helped me understand better how a Java application can communicate with an external API and use the data it gets back.
Exercises # For this week I made a small project using the TMDB API as my wednesday assignment.
Week 3 exercise on GitHub
title: Week 3 - Data Integration

content:
Week 4 - Concurrency # In week 4 I worked with concurrency and learned how threads work in Java.
I learned that threads can be used to run multiple tasks at the same time insteead of doing everything one by one.
We also worked with ExecutorService, which can be used to manage multiple threads.
Another thing I learned about was race conditions. This can happen when two threads try to use or change the same data at the same time, which can cause problems.
In our backend project “DriveApp”, I added threads to the booking system. We made a test where two students tried to book the same driving lesson at the same time.
I used ExecutorService with two threads and made the bookLesson method synchronized, so only one student could book the lesson.
Overall, this week helped me understand concurrency better and how threads can be useful in a real backend project.
Exercises # During the week I worked with concurrency in our DriveApp backend project.
I added threads to the booking system so two students could not book the same driving lesson at the same time.
DriveApp backend project on GitHub
title: Week 4 - Concurrency

content:
Week 5 REST API # In week 5 I started working with REST APIs and learned how to create endpoints using Javalin.
I worked with the different HTTP methods GET, POST, PUT and DELETE and learned how they are used to get, create, update and delete data.
I also learned more about HTTP status codes and how an API should return the correct response when something works or when an error happens.
During the week I worked with a Dog API where I created different endpoints for dogs. I tested the endpoints by getting a dog by id, creating new dogs, updating dogs and deleting them.
Later in the week I worked on a Poem API where I connected the REST API to a PostgreSQL database using JPA and Hibernate.
I created a Poem entity and worked with the API setup, database configuration and error handling. I also added poems to the database and used the API to work with the stored data.
Overall, this week helped me understand how a REST API is structured and how it can communicate with a database.
Exercises # During the week I worked on a Dog REST API where I practiced creating and testing GET, POST, PUT and DELETE endpoints with Javalin.
REST API Project on GitHub
I also worked on a Poem API where I connected the API to PostgreSQL using JPA and Hibernate and stored poems in the database.
Poem API on GitHub
title: Week 5 REST API

content:
Week 5 - SP-1 Movie Repository # In week 5 I worked on the SP-1 Movie Repository project together with my group. The project was about creating a backend application that gets Danish movie data from the TMDb API and stores it in a PostgreSQL database.
We worked with movies, actors, directors and genres and created entities and relationships between them using JPA and Hibernate. We also used DTOs for the data from the API and worked with DAO and service classes to keep the project more structured.
The application could search for movies, find movies by genre and show things like the highest rated, lowest rated and most popular movies. We also worked with JUnit and Testcontainers to test parts of the backend.
At the end of the project we made a small video where we presented the project and explained some of the code we had worked on.
Overall, this project helped me use many of the things we had learned in the previous weeks in one bigger backend project.
Project # I worked on this project together with my group, which consisted of me, Musa, Khattab & Rasull.
SP-1 Movie Repository on GitHub

content:
Week 7 - Security # This week, we focused on security in REST APIs and how to protect applications from unauthorized access. We learned about password hashing using BCrypt, authentication, authorization, and JSON Web Tokens (JWT).
We started by learning how to securely store passwords using BCrypt instead of plain text. We also worked with creating a security layer to manage users and roles.
During Wednesday’s CodeLab, I worked on implementing security in a Hotel API using Java, Javalin, Hibernate, and PostgreSQL. We created User and Role entities and worked with authentication and database relationships.
On Thursday, we focused on JWT and how tokens are used to authenticate users and protect API endpoints.
I also worked on implementing BCrypt password hashing and JWT authentication in our group project, DriveApp, which is our biggest project this semester. DriveApp is a driving school management application, and adding security is an important step in making the application more secure.
GitHub: DriveApp
Overall this week helped me understand how backend security works in practice and how to implement authentication and password protection in a real project.
title: Week 7 - Security

content:
DriveApp – Driving School Management System # DriveApp is our third semester backend project, which I developed together with Musa.
The idea behind DriveApp was to create a system for a driving school where students, instructors, driving lessons and bookings could be managed in one place.
We built the application using Java, Javalin, Hibernate/JPA and PostgreSQL.
During the semester, we worked on the project step by step and added new features as we learned about different backend topics.
We started by setting up our database and working with JPA. Later, we added REST API endpoints, integrated Google Gemini as an AI driving assistant, worked with security using JWT and BCrypt, and created automated tests.
In the end, we also worked with Docker, GitHub Actions and deployed our backend to DigitalOcean.
On this page, I will go through how we developed DriveApp throughout the semester, what I learned and how we used the different technologies in our project.

Project Development # During the semester, we worked on DriveApp step by step and used what we learned from the different backend topics in class.
Each week, we learned something new that we could use to improve our application. We started with databases and JPA, and later worked with REST APIs, testing, security and deployment.
The table below shows the topics we worked with each week and how we used them in DriveApp.
Week Topic How we used it in DriveApp Week 1 JPA Basics We used Hibernate, JPA and PostgreSQL to set up our database and create our first entities and DAO classes. Week 2 JPA Relations We created relationships between Student, Instructor, Lesson and Booking, and worked with JPQL queries. Week 3 Data Integration We integrated Google Gemini using Java HttpClient, JSON and DTOs to create our AI driving assistant. Week 4 Concurrency We worked with threads, race conditions and synchronized in our booking system, and CompletableFuture for Gemini. Week 5 REST API We used Javalin to create routes, controllers and endpoints for students, instructors, lessons and bookings. Week 6 REST Testing We used JUnit, REST Assured and Testcontainers to test our API endpoints and database operations. Week 7 Security We implemented BCrypt, JWT authentication and role based access control to protect our API. Week 8 Deployment & DevOps We used Docker, GitHub Actions and DigitalOcean, and followed the deployment guide to connect our domain through DanDomain. Below, I will go through each week in more detail and explain what we worked on, what I learned and how DriveApp developed throughout the semester.
Selected Blog Posts # Below are my blog posts from the third semester, where I have documented what we worked on in class and what I learned each week.
These posts show my learning throughout the semester, while the sections below explain how we used these topics in DriveApp.
Weekly Blog Posts # Week 1 - JPA Basics Week 2 - JPA Relations Week 3 - Data Integration Week 4 - Concurrency Week 5 - REST API Week 6 - REST Testing Week 7 - Security Week 8 - Deployment Week 1 – JPA Basics # In week 1, we started working on DriveApp and focused on setting up the backend and database.
We used Java, Maven, Hibernate/JPA and PostgreSQL. We also started creating our first entities and DAO classes to manage data in the database.
What we worked on # Set up our Java project with Maven Connected our application to PostgreSQL Configured Hibernate and JPA Created Student and Instructor entities Worked with DAO classes and CRUD operations Used EntityManager to communicate with the database What I learned # This week I learned how JPA and Hibernate work together with PostgreSQL and how we can use entities to represent database tables.
I also got a better understanding of DAO classes and why it is useful to separate database operations from the rest of the application.
Result # By the end of the week, we had the basic database setup ready and could start managing data through our DAO classes.
This gave us a good starting point for developing the rest of DriveApp.
Week 2 – JPA Relations # In week 2, we continued working on DriveApp and focused on creating relationships between our entities.
We worked with Student, Instructor, Lesson and Booking, and connected them using JPA relationships.
This was important for our project because students need to be connected to their bookings, and driving lessons need to be connected to instructors.
What we worked on # Created relationships between our entities Worked with @OneToMany and @ManyToOne Connected students, instructors, lessons and bookings Used foreign keys to connect database tables Worked with JPQL queries Updated our DAO classses Created JUnit tests for CRUD operations and relationships What I learned # This week I learned how relationships work in JPA and how we can connect different entities in our database.
I also learned how to use JPQL to retrieve data and how important it is to structure database relationships correctly.
Working with JUnit tests also helped me understand how to check that our database operations work as expected.
Result # By the end of the week, we had created relationships between the different entities in DriveApp.
We could now connect students to bookings and instructors to driving lessons.
This made our database more useful and gave us a better foundation for building the booking system later in the project.
Week 3 – Data Integration & Gemini AI # In week 3, we worked with data integration and started adding Google Gemini to DriveApp.
We wanted to create an AI driving assistant where students could ask questions about driving theory, traffic rules and road safety.
To make this work, we used Java HttpClient to communicate with the Gemini API and JSON to send and receive data.
What we worked on # Integrated Google Gemini into DriveApp Created the DrivingAiService class Used Java HttpClient to send HTTP requests Worked with JSON and Jackson ObjectMapper Created DTO classes to handle the Gemini response Worked with serialization and deserialization Created tests for our AI service What I learned # This week I learned how to connect our Java application to an external API.
I also got a better understanding of how JSON works and how we can use Jackson to convert JSON into Java objects.
Working with DTOs helped me understand how to structure data when communicating with external services.
Result # By the end of the week, we had implemented our AI driving assistant using Google Gemini.
Our application could now send questions to Gemini and receive answers that could be used in DriveApp.
This was an important feature because it added something extra to our driving school system.
Week 4 – Concurrency & Booking System # In week 4, we worked with concurrency and multithreading in Java.
We learned how multiple threads can run at the same time and what problems can happen when different users try to access or change the same data.
This was relevant for DriveApp because we have a booking system where multiple students might try to book the same driving lesson.
We also worked with CompletableFuture in our Gemini AI integration to handle asynchronous HTTP requests.
What we worked on # Learned about threads and multithreading in Java Worked with Runnable and ExecutorService Learned about race conditions Worked with synchronized Developed our BookingService class Added checks to prevent students from booking an already booked lesson Worked with CompletableFuture in our DrivingAiService Tested different booking scenarios What I learned # This week I learned how concurrency works and why it is important when multiple users are using the same application.
I also learned about race conditions and how synchronized can help prevent multiple threads from accessing the same critical section at the same time.
Working with CompletableFuture helped me understand how asynchronous operations can be used when communicating with external APIs like Google Gemini.
Result # By the end of the week, we had improved our booking system by checking if a driving lesson was already booked before creating a new booking.
We also worked with concurrency to better understand how to handle multiple requests.
This helped us make DriveApp more reliable and gave us a better understanding of concurrency in backend applications.
Week 5 – REST API & Javalin # In week 5, we worked with REST APIs and started making our DriveApp backend accessible through HTTP requests.
Until now, we had mainly worked with our database, entities and DAO classes. We now wanted to make it possible to interact with our application through API endpoints.
We used Javalin to create our REST API and connected our controllers to the DAO classes.
What we worked on # Added Javalin to our project Created routes and controllers Worked with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE requests Created endpoints for students, instructors, lessons and bookings Connected our controllers to the DAO layer Used DTOs to handle request and response data Added validation for incoming requests Worked with HTTP status codes Added error handling and logging Documented our API endpoints in the README What I learned # This week I learned how REST APIs work and how we can use HTTP methods to communicate with our backend.
I also learned why it is important to separate our application into different layers.
Routes define the endpoints, controllers handle the requests, and DAO classes communicate with the database.
Working with DTOs also helped me understand how we can control what data is sent and received through our API.
Result # By the end of the week, we had created a REST API for DriveApp using Javalin.
We could now manage students, instructors, driving lessons and bookings through HTTP requests.
This was an important step because our application was no longer only connected to the database but could also be accessed through API endpoints.
Week 6 – REST Testing & Integration Tests # In week 6, we focused on testing our DriveApp backend to make sure everything worked as expected.
We had already worked with tests for our DAO classes, but now we also wanted to test our REST API endpoints.
We used JUnit and REST Assured to send HTTP requests and check if our API returned the correct responses.
We also worked with two separate databases, one for production and one for testing. This was important because we did not want our tests to affect the real data in our production database.
What we worked on # Used JUnit to create automated tests Used REST Assured to test our API endpoints Tested GET, POST, PUT and DELETE requests Checked HTTP status codes and JSON responses Tested both valid and invalid requests Created tests for students, instructors, lessons and bookings Worked with Testcontainers and PostgreSQL for database testing Created a separate local PostgreSQL database for testing Updated our database configuration to connect to the test database Made sure our tests did not affect the production database Used test data without adding test users or bookings to production Tested our DAO classes and database operations Created tests for our Gemini AI integration Worked with error handling and different test scenarios What I learned # This week I learned how important automated testing is when developing a backend application.
I learned how to use REST Assured to test API endpoints without having to send requests manually.
I also got a better understanding of how Testcontainers can be used to test our application with PostgreSQL.
One important thing we worked on was separating our production database from our test database.
We created a local PostgreSQL test database and changed our configuration so the tests would use the correct database.
We did this because we did not want our tests to create test users, bookings or other test data in the production database.
This helped me understand why it is important to use different database configurations for testing and production.
Testing different scenarios also helped me understand how to find errors and make sure our API handles invalid requests correctly.
Result # By the end of the week, we had added more automated tests to DriveApp.
We could now test our REST API, DAO classes and different parts of our application.
We also got our tests running with a separate test database, so we could test our API without affecting the production data.
This made our testing setup safer and helped us avoid filling the production database with test users and bookings.
Overall, this made it easier to find problems when changing our code and helped us make DriveApp more reliable.
Week 7 – Security, BCrypt & JWT # In week 7, we worked with security in DriveApp and focused on making our REST API more secure.
We wanted to make sure that students and instructors could log in safely and only access the features they were allowed to use.
To do this, we worked with BCrypt for password hashing and JWT for authentication.
What we worked on # Implemented BCrypt to hash passwords Created login functionality for students and instructors Worked with authentication and authorization Implemented JWT tokens for logged in users Created the JWTToken class Added security filters to protect our API endpoints Worked with different user roles such as STUDENT and INSTRUCTOR Added role based access control Added checks so students can only access their own information Created tests for BCrypt and JWT What I learned # This week I learned the difference between authentication and authorization.
Authentication is about checking who the user is, while authorization is about checking what the user is allowed to do.
I also learned why we should never store passwords as plain text and how BCrypt can be used to hash passwords before saving them in the database.
Working with JWT helped me understand how a user can log in and use a token to access protected API endpoints.
Result # By the end of the week, we had added security to DriveApp using BCrypt, JWT and different user roles.
Students and instructors could now log in, and our backend could check their permissions before allowing access to protected endpoints.
This was an important part of the project because we needed to protect user information and make sure that users could only access the features they were allowed to use.
Week 8 – Deployment & DevOps # In week 8, we worked with deployment and DevOps to make DriveApp available online.
Until now, we had mainly been running our application locally. We wanted to make our backend accessible through the internet so other people could use our API.
To do this, we followed the deployment guide from our course material and used Docker, GitHub Actions, DigitalOcean and DanDomain.
What we worked on # Created a Dockerfile for our Java application Worked with Docker images and containers Used Docker Compose to manage our application and database Created a GitHub Actions workflow Worked with CI/CD to automate building and testing Used Docker Hub to store our Docker images Followed the deployment guide from our course material Deployed DriveApp to a DigitalOcean server Configured PostgreSQL for our deployed application Worked with environment variables Used DanDomain to configure our domain and DNS settings Connected our domain to the DigitalOcean server Set up HTTPS for our API Tested our deployed REST API What I learned # This week I learned how to deploy a backend application and make it available online.
I learned how Docker can be used to package our application into a container so it can run in different environments.
Working with GitHub Actions also helped me understand how CI/CD works and how we can automate building and testing our application when we push changes to GitHub.
We also followed the deployment guide from our course material to get DriveApp up and running using DigitalOcean and DanDomain.
This helped me understand how to connect a domain to our server and how DNS settings work. It was also nice to see our application running online instead of only on localhost.
Result # By the end of the week, we had deployed DriveApp to DigitalOcean and made our REST API available online.
Our backend can now be accessed through our domain:
DriveApp API
We also had a GitHub Actions workflow that helped automate our build and testing process.
This was an important step because we went from running DriveApp locally to having a backend that could be accessed through the internet.
Project Architecture & Technical Decisions # In DriveApp, we used a layered architecture to keep our backend organized and easier to maintain.
We separated our application into routes, controllers, DAO classes and services, so each part of the code has its own responsibility.
REST API and Database # We used Javalin to create our REST API and handle HTTP requests for students, instructors, lessons and bookings.
We also used Hibernate/JPA and PostgreSQL to store our data. DAO classes handle the database operations, while DTOs control what data is sent and received through our API.
This made our code easier to understand and helped us avoid exposing sensitive information like passwords.
Services and Booking Logic # We created service classes like BookingService to handle booking logic and DrivingAiService to communicate with Google Gemini.
Separating this logic from our controllers made the application easier to organize and maintain.
Separate Test and Production Databases # We decided to use separate databases for production and testing.
We created a local PostgreSQL test database and updated our configuration so our REST Assured tests would use the test database.
This was important because we did not want test users or bookings to affect our production database.
Security # We used BCrypt to hash passwords and JWT to authenticate users.
We also implemented roles for students and instructors to control which endpoints they could access.
We chose these solutions to protect user information and make our API more secure.
Deployment # We used Docker to run our application in containers and GitHub Actions to automate building and testing.
We also followed the deployment guide from our course material and used DigitalOcean and DanDomain to get DriveApp online.
What I learned # Working with DriveApp helped me understand why it is important to think about the structure of an application and not just make the code work.
I also learned how decisions about security, testing and deployment can make a backend more reliable and easier to maintain.
Final Reflection # Throughout the semester, I have learned a lot about backend development by working on DriveApp together with Musa.
We started with JPA, Hibernate and PostgreSQL, and slowly built our application by adding REST APIs, testing, security and deployment.
One of the biggest things I learned was how the different parts of a backend application work together, from the database and DAO classes to controllers and API endpoints.
We also faced some challenges during the project, especially with testing and getting our application to work correctly with different database configurations.
For example, we had to set up a separate test database so our REST Assured tests would not affect our production data. We also spent time fixing issues with our tests and GitHub Actions.
Another challenge we had was with our domain from DanDomain. We had problems getting the DNS settings to work correctly, especially with the nameservers (NS1, NS2 and NS3).
We had to contact DanDomain several times and call back and forth to figure out what was wrong and get the domain connected correctly to our server.
This was a bit frustrating, but it helped me understand more about how domains, nameservers and DNS work when deploying an application.
Working on these problems helped me understand how important testing, debugging and having a good project structure are.
I also learned how to work with GitHub in a group and how to deploy a backend application using Docker and DigitalOcean.
Overall, DriveApp has helped me get a better understanding of backend development and how to build an application from the beginning to a working deployed system.
